readerTitle: The app that isn't dying, and isn't growing
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가계용 장보기 앱, 소형 부품 제조사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 정체된 사업에서는 전체 숫자보다 '떠나지 않는 소수'가 무엇을 하는지를 먼저 보고, 계속할지·방향을 바꿀지·접을지를 기한과 함께 정한다.
misconception: 매출이 조금이라도 나고 망하지 않았으니 조금만 더 버티거나 광고·기능을 늘리면 다시 성장할 것이다.

cards.title: The app that isn't dying, and isn't growing
body: Mira built a shared grocery-list app for households. Eighteen months in, it has 4,000 sign-ups and $1,200 a month in revenue. Servers cost $400. Mira pays herself nothing.
Every month looks like the last. Nothing is on fire, but nothing is moving either.

image.label: A flat line on a phone screen beside a grocery list
image.brief: 부엌 식탁 위 스마트폰. 화면에 수평으로 쭉 이어지는 그래프 선, 옆에 반쯤 쓴 장보기 목록 메모지. 차분하지만 정체된 분위기. 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Mira do first?
body: She has savings for about nine more months. Friends say she should push harder. Her list of feature requests keeps growing.

options.text: Spend $3,000 on ads to restart growth
options.feedback: Ads bring more people into the same leaky product. If most users drift away, she pays to learn what she already knows.

options.text: Study the users who stayed and what they actually do
options.feedback: This is **when to pivot** at work: the signal comes from behavior, not from effort. The few who stay often point to the real business.

options.text: Build the three most requested features
options.feedback: Requests show interest, but they may come from people who will leave anyway. Building first spends months before she knows who the product is for.

cards.title: The loyal users weren't households.
body: Most families used the app for a few weeks, then stopped. But about 60 accounts opened it every day.
Mira called a dozen of them. They were small caterers and meal-prep kitchens. Staff used the shared list to track supplier orders across shifts. Several said they'd pay more for it.
The product she built for homes was quietly doing a job for kitchens.

image.label: Many fading home icons and a few bright kitchen icons
image.brief: 화면 가득 흐려지는 집 아이콘들 사이에 밝게 빛나는 주방(요리사 모자, 냄비) 아이콘 몇 개. 대비를 강하게.

cards.title: Why "not dead" is the trap.
body: Mira's app is a **zombie**: it earns enough to keep running, but not enough to grow or pay its founder.
Zombies feel safe because nothing forces a decision. Meanwhile the real cost piles up: her time, her savings, and the other things she could be building.
Naming the zombie is useful. It turns "keep going" from a default into a choice she has to justify.

cards.title: Which change fits what she found?
body: Mira decides to change direction. She has three options on the table.

options.text: Rebuild for small food kitchens: same core list, new customer, business pricing
options.feedback: A **customer segment pivot**, one of the pivot types: keep what works, change who it serves. It follows the evidence without throwing away the product.

options.text: Keep households and add a paid business tier on the side
options.feedback: Lower risk, but it splits her time between a group that leaves and one that stays. Half a pivot can keep the zombie alive.

options.text: Build a full kitchen platform: orders, staff rotas, inventory
options.feedback: It goes far beyond what 60 kitchens proved they want. A big leap costs months before any new signal arrives.

cards.title: Sixty users is a clue, not proof.
body: A small loyal group can be real demand or a lucky coincidence. Mira should test before she rebuilds: sell to 20 new kitchens by hand and see who pays.
She also needs a **stop rule**. For example: if fewer than ten kitchens pay within 90 days, she shuts down well, telling users early and helping them export their lists.
A pivot without a deadline can become a new zombie.

cards.title: Now it's a parts factory.
body: A small factory makes metal brackets for e-bike brands. Orders have been flat for two years. The line covers its costs but earns almost nothing.
One customer, a warehouse-equipment firm, reorders every month for its conveyor systems. What should the owner do?

options.text: Keep running the line as is; it isn't losing money
options.feedback: That's the **zombie** pattern. The line ties up machines and staff that could serve a growing market.

options.text: Spend 90 days pitching conveyor and warehouse firms, with a clear stop rule
options.feedback: It reads the loyal customer as a signal for **when to pivot** and tests a customer segment pivot before committing.
Decisive, and sometimes right. But it walks away from the one customer pointing to a better market.

cards.title: Stalled is a decision waiting to be made.
body: Look at who stays, name the zombie, test the change, and set a deadline.
**Try it today:** pick one flat product or line. Write down who uses it most, what they use it for, and the date by which you'll decide.
list: **When to pivot:** read the signal in who stays
**Zombie companies:** "not dead" still has a cost
**Types of pivots:** change the customer, keep what works
